title: Mudita
hookLine: sympathetic joy: gladness at someone else's good fortune
last: ANGULIMALA — THEY ARE HEADING FOR PAIN.

lines: A SMALL FLICKER: WHY NOT ME?
cards: A friend texts: I got the job. Or: we're engaged. Or: the scan was clear.
For a split second, before you type the exclamation points, something happens inside. Sometimes it's pure gladness. Sometimes there's a small, uninvited flicker: why not me?

Its darker cousin, pleasure at someone else's trouble, is familiar enough that English borrowed a German word for it. For the good opposite, joy at someone else's good fortune, English has no everyday word at all.

teach.b: Mudita comes from a root meaning to be glad, to rejoice. It's usually translated sympathetic joy, or appreciative joy: gladness at another's happiness and success. It's the third of the four rooms.

teach.h: THE MARK: GLADNESS; THE JOB: NO ENVY.
teach.b: The Visuddhimagga's map says mudita's mark is gladness, and its job is to be free of envy. It shows up as the end of discontent, the sour feeling that someone else's good news somehow takes something away from you.
Its ground is seeing other people's success. Here's what makes mudita unusual. Kindness wishes that people be happy.
Compassion wishes that they be free from pain. Mudita meets people who already are happy, and simply agrees.

teach.h: JOY YOU DIDN'T HAVE TO EARN.
teach.b: It's joy you didn't have to earn, available every time anyone, anywhere, has a good day.
Some teachers call it the most overlooked of the four rooms, because people assume they'd feel it naturally, and then discover the little flicker of why not me. The manual's advice is practical.
Start with someone you're already close to, a dear friend whose good news makes you easily glad.
Then widen the circle: a neutral person, then someone difficult. And practice when you see someone happy, or hear good news about them, so the gladness has something real to rest on.

This week walked through two and a half rooms: the four divine abodes; metta and its near enemy, clinging; its far enemy, ill will; karuna, the trembling heart; pity, which looks down, and compassion, which sits beside; compassion even for the one who harms.

how: Buddhists practice mudita by rejoicing in others' happiness and good deeds; in many Theravada communities people say 'sadhu, sadhu, sadhu' to rejoice in someone else's merit, and teachers offer mudita as a meditation starting with a dear friend.

o: pleasure at a rival's bad luck or failure
the calm happiness that comes from meditation
gladness at someone else's good fortune

games.q: a friend texts: 'I got the job!' you feel a flicker of 'why not me?' what does mudita look like?
o: pretend you didn't see the text.
notice the flicker, then let yourself be glad with them.
reply with a story about your own success.
games.why: mudita's job, the manual says, is to be free of envy: notice the flicker, and let their joy be joy.

practice: Bring to mind a dear friend who's had good news lately, or who's simply happy right now, and picture their face when things are going well.

Let yourself be glad with them, notice how that gladness feels in your own body, and if words help, offer one: may your happiness continue. If you like, widen it to someone you barely know, enjoying a good day.

wordCard.voice: Mudita. Sympathetic joy: gladness at someone else's good fortune, joy you didn't have to earn.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit muditā: sympathetic joy, the third divine abode.

carryVoice: Your line: their joy is joy. And it can be yours too. That's the week.
